svg.title: DSA Backward Determinism — Bounded Waves and Two-Fold Shards
svg.desc: An English source-audited diagram explaining the 128 CTA bounded-wave schedule, one-writer-per-shard mapping, deterministic 128 to 16 to 1 reduction, and how removing in-grid semaphore waits avoids a potential scheduling deadlock.
svg.text: Bounded Q waves + private FP32 shards + a fixed two-fold reduction
Bound the dependency domain: one launch = at most 128 Q CTAs

g.text: CTA completion order may vary — writes never collide
Same wave: CTA i is the sole writer of shard i
Across waves: stream completion orders reuse
After BWD: folds start only when all waves finish
Therefore no concurrent writers need arbitration
no conflict → no ticket, lock, or spin loop
Proof: every CTA in a wave writes a different shard
N = 128, wave w, CTA lane i ∈ {0, ..., N−1}
shard(w,i) = q(w,i) mod N = (N·w + i) mod N = i
Tail wave: i < r ≤ 128, so the same injective mapping still holds.
Why not an FA4-style semaphore for DSA dKV?
FA4’s protocol is valid; the mismatch is DSA’s irregular sparse fan-out.
up to Top-K KV rows and
Sharding replaces temporal arbitration with spatial separation; one fixed fold pays the ordering cost once.
All BWD waves finish before reduction. Both folds use a fixed FP32 addition order.
FOLD 1 · sum each 8-shard group in index order
Same inputs + same FP32 addition tree = bitwise-stable dKV output
If waiters occupy all slots, the predecessor cannot run
Bounded wave: no in-grid wait edge
No spin loop; any scheduled CTA can progress
A successor is never resident before its wave
dQ: single writer · dSink: one CTA/head with fixed traversal
